READING

**Building the numbers season by season**

The Vantwyn gross payment is 400 × £168 = £67,200 a season. Against that sit three costs:

| Item | Calculation | Per season |
|---|---|---|
| Borage forgone | 400 × £71 | £28,400 |
| Spray-loss replacements | 0.09 × 400 × £210 | £7,560 |
| Haulage and labour | given | £6,900 |
| **Total cost** | | **£42,860** |
| **Net per season** | | **£24,340** |

Three seasons therefore yield an operating surplus of £73,020.

**The equipment question is the pivot**

TREVANNOCK keeps the pallets and lorry working and realises roughly £20,000 for them after the permit lapses at the end of 2029. ORMSCLEUCH takes £96,000 from Ravensgate now. The gap between those two exit values is £76,000.

Undiscounted comparison over the three-year horizon:

- TREVANNOCK advantage from operating: +£73,020
- TREVANNOCK disadvantage on equipment realisation: −£76,000
- **Net position: ORMSCLEUCH ahead by £2,980**

That is before any time-value adjustment. Even a 3–4 % discount rate on the annual Vantwyn surpluses widens ORMSCLEUCH's financial lead to roughly £10,000–£13,000. The money arithmetic is close but consistently favours ORMSCLEUCH.

**Risk sits entirely on the TREVANNOCK side**

The 9 % spray-loss figure comes from a single observed season at Whinnerdale Bees and is probably the central estimate, not the worst case. Vantwyn will not alter its programme, so there is no mechanism to improve on it. A 12–15 % loss year converts that £24,340 seasonal net into a much smaller number or a loss. Replacement colonies also enter the apiary at lower productivity than established stock, which creates a drag on honey yield not fully captured in the £210 replacement cost alone.

**The previous track record matters**

All three of the contracts that originally justified the £187,000 investment failed to renew. That history does not doom Vantwyn, but it does mean the assumption of smooth, full three-season delivery deserves scepticism. A contract that terminates early, or that produces heavier-than-expected losses, closes the gap or eliminates it entirely.

**The Coldharbour/Nyefield option is weak under TREVANNOCK**

Under TREVANNOCK, 400 of 640 colonies are committed to Vantwyn from April each year. Any vale grower needing spring pollination would be competing for the same 400 colonies at the same time. The remaining 240 are unlikely to make a commercially attractive offer to clients of that kind. Coldharbour and Nyefield represent genuine optionality only if capacity exists to serve them, and it does not under a full Vantwyn commitment—at least not until 2030, by which point the lorry permit has gone and a new vehicle would be needed to stay in the vale.

**ORMSCLEUCH as the positive case, not just the default**

The £96,000 lands before 2026-11-28, is certain, and is immediately productive (reducing debt or earning investment return). All 640 colonies run on home heather and borage, a model that generated £143,000 last season with no haulage and no spray-programme dependency. The business becomes structurally simpler: one revenue stream, one management focus, no logistics tail. The queen-rearing shed (not part of the Ravensgate offer) remains as an asset supporting colony replacement from within.

**What ORMSCLEUCH costs**

It exits a market where two growers are already asking for prices. That is a real cost. But staying for three years under Vantwyn's terms does not maintain access to those growers—capacity is already full—and by 2030 the permit cliff would require fresh capital investment to remain in the vale anyway.

**Conclusion**

The three-season operating surplus from TREVANNOCK (£73,020) is almost exactly consumed by the fall in equipment realisable value (£76,000 differential). The finances are a draw at best, with time-value and spray-risk weighting both pushing against TREVANNOCK. ORMSCLEUCH is the cleaner call.

---

CALL
ORMSCLEUCH

GROUNDS
The three-season Vantwyn operating surplus (£73,020) is almost exactly cancelled by the £76,000 fall in equipment realisable value between now and the permit expiry, leaving TREVANNOCK financially neutral at best while carrying unmitigatable spray-loss risk that ORMSCLEUCH avoids entirely.
